name: Substantive Testing at Full Coverage
title: Substantive Testing at Full Coverage
answer: Substantive testing at full coverage means audit procedures that examine every item in a population rather than a sample, typically for transactions, balances, or disclosures where risk is high or populations are small enough to test completely. In continuous audit, it extends beyond year-end to ongoing monitoring, so exceptions can be flagged as they occur. It covers tests of details, confirmations, recalculations, and inspection of supporting records, with the aim of obtaining evidence about completeness, accuracy, and existence. It is not a substitute for understanding the business or assessing risk, and it does not replace professional judgment about materiality.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Substantive testing at full coverage means audit procedures that examine every item in a population rather than a sample, typically for transactions, balances, or disclosures where risk is high or populations are small enough to test completely. In continuous audit, it extends beyond year-end to ongoing monitoring, so exceptions can be flagged as they occur. It covers tests of details, confirmations, recalculations, and inspection of supporting records, with the aim of obtaining evidence about completeness, accuracy, and existence. It is not a substitute for understanding the business or assessing risk, and it does not replace professional judgment about materiality.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Full coverage substantive testing depends on reliable access to complete data populations from ERP, subledgers, bank feeds, and document repositories. It runs on data pipelines that extract, standardize, and reconcile records, often using audit data analytics platforms, SQL, Python, or built-in tools in ERP and GRC systems. Controls over data completeness and integrity are essential, because testing every item only works if the population itself is complete and accurate. Storage and compute need to handle large volumes, and audit trails must record what was tested, when, and from which source.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The auditor defines the population and the assertion, then writes or configures procedures that apply the same test to every item, such as matching invoices to purchase orders and receipts, recalculating depreciation, or scanning journals for unusual combinations. Exceptions are investigated, and results are aggregated to evaluate misstatement. Sampling risk is removed for the tested population, but other risks remain, including data quality, logic errors, and the possibility that the procedure does not address the assertion. Documentation includes the procedure logic, parameters, and evidence of review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Full coverage testing raises questions about access rights to source systems, privacy of personal data in the population, and the provenance of data used as evidence. Audit teams need to document data lineage, retention, and permissions, and to consider whether automated procedures create a record that can be defended to regulators or in litigation. The site's 215 compliance and regulation pages sit alongside this work, because rules on audit evidence and data protection keep changing. Where AI is used to select or prioritize exceptions, the model's logic and limitations should be documented and reviewed. Professional standards still require supervision, review, and a conclusion on sufficiency and appropriateness of evidence.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: As systems become more interoperable and data more standardized, full coverage testing is likely to move from periodic projects to always-on assurance, with dashboards that show exceptions in near real time. AI may help classify transactions, detect anomalies, and draft workpapers, but the auditor remains responsible for the conclusion. The main constraint is not compute but data quality, access, and the ability to explain automated results to stakeholders. The site tracks 147 active AI lawsuits, and liability and evidence questions around automated testing will keep developing alongside the technology.
